claim: Formation of a specialized wound epidermis is required to initiate salamander limb regeneration.
source: Formation of a specialized wound epidermis is required to initiate salamander limb regeneration.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by citations to classical literature throughout the manuscript.

claim: Midkine (mk) acts as a critical survival signal to control the expansion and function of the early wound epidermis.
source: Through loss- and gain-of-function experiments, we demonstrate that mk acts as both a critical survival signal to control the expansion and function of the early wound epidermis and an anti-inflammatory cytokine to resolve early injury-induced inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TUNEL staining showing increased cell death in the wound epidermis of mk loss-of-function contexts (Figure 5), and wound epidermis thickness measurements (Figure 4).

claim: Midkine (mk) acts as an anti-inflammatory cytokine to resolve early injury-induced inflammation.
source: Through loss- and gain-of-function experiments, we demonstrate that mk acts as both a critical survival signal to control the expansion and function of the early wound epidermis and an anti-inflammatory cytokine to resolve early injury-induced inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing higher monocyte densities in both mk loss-of-function and gain-of-function contexts (Figure 6F-I, Figure 7K-M).

claim: Salamanders form a blastema, a transient cellular structure comprised of progenitors derived from different non-epithelial tissues that eventually reconstructs the new limb.
source: While most mammals respond to traumatic limb injuries including amputation with a fibrotic scarring response, salamanders instead form a blastema, a transient cellular structure comprised of progenitors derived from different non-epithelial tissues (muscle, connective tissue etc.) that eventually reconstructs the new limb (Kragl et al., 2009; Sandoval-Guzmán et al., 2014; Fei et al., 2017; Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Initiation of blastema formation requires the presence of a wound epidermis for both formation and maintenance of the blastema.
source: Classical salamander limb regenerative experiments determined that initiation of blastema formation requires the presence of a wound epidermis for both formation and maintenance of the blastema (Goss, 1956a; Thornton, 1957; Thornton, 1958; Mescher, 1976; Tassava and Garling, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical experimental literature.

claim: Epithelial cells from the intact peripheral skin migrate radially over the exposed stump tissues and form a thin wound epithelium covering the amputation plane within 12 hours post-amputation.
source: Immediately post-amputation, epithelial cells from the intact peripheral skin migrate radially over the exposed stump tissues and form a thin wound epithelium covering the amputation plane within 12 hours (Hay and Fischman, 1961).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The wound epidermis only contains an epithelial layer comprised primarily of keratinocytes, allowing for direct communication between the wound epidermis and underlying stump tissues.
source: Unlike normal full thickness skin that contains two layers (epidermis and dermis), the wound epidermis only contains an epithelial layer comprised primarily of keratinocytes, allowing for direct communication between the wound epidermis and underlying stump tissues (Repesh and Oberpriller, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The early wound epithelium gradually expands into a stratified epidermis called the apical epithelial cap (AEC) as the blastema forms during later stages of regeneration.
source: As the blastema forms during later stages of regeneration, the early wound epithelium gradually expands into a stratified epidermis commonly called the apical epithelial cap (AEC), which is a signaling structure that maintains blastemal outgrowth and directs patterning (Boilly and Albert, 1990; Christensen and Tassava, 2000; Han et al., 2001; Christensen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The AEC is a signaling structure that maintains blastemal outgrowth and directs patterning.
source: As the blastema forms during later stages of regeneration, the early wound epithelium gradually expands into a stratified epidermis commonly called the apical epithelial cap (AEC), which is a signaling structure that maintains blastemal outgrowth and directs patterning (Boilly and Albert, 1990; Christensen and Tassava, 2000; Han et al., 2001; Christensen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AEC expansion occurs primarily via proliferation and subsequent distal migration of epithelial cells in the peripheral skin.
source: This expansion occurs primarily via proliferation and subsequent distal migration of epithelial cells in the peripheral skin (Hay and Fischman, 1961; Campbell and Crews, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inhibiting early wound epidermis formation by suturing or grafting full thickness skin over the amputation plane blocked blastema formation.
source: Classical studies showed that inhibiting early wound epidermis formation by either suturing or grafting full thickness skin over the amputation plane (Mescher, 1976; Tassava and Garling, 1979) or immediately inserting the amputated limb into the body cavity (Goss, 1956a) blocked blastema formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical experimental literature.

claim: If the amputated limb was inserted into the body cavity after the wound epidermis formed, regeneration proceeded normally.
source: However, if the amputated limb was inserted into the body cavity after the wound epidermis formed, regeneration proceeded normally, demonstrating an early need for the wound epithelium (Goss, 1956b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Preventing AEC development by continuous removal of the wound epidermis hindered limb regeneration.
source: Furthermore, preventing AEC development by either continuous removal of the wound epidermis (Thornton, 1957) or daily irradiation to inhibit proliferative expansion also hindered limb regeneration (Thornton, 1958).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The AEC expresses mitogens and patterning factors that help to maintain blastemal cell proliferation and pattern the regenerate.
source: The AEC expresses mitogens and patterning factors that help to maintain blastemal cell proliferation and pattern the regenerate (Boilly and Albert, 1990; Campbell and Crews, 2008; Ghosh et al., 2008; Satoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Preventing early wound epidermis formation affected the maintenance, but not the onset of proliferation of progenitors.
source: Preventing early wound epidermis formation was shown to affect the maintenance, but not the onset of proliferation of progenitors (Mescher, 1976; Tassava and Garling, 1979; Johnson et al., 2018), though it is worth noting that the early wound epidermis does express molecules capable of inducing proliferation (Sugiura et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some dedifferentiation of muscle, bone and cartilage tissue was still observed when wound epidermis formation was prevented, although not to the same extent as normal regenerating limbs.
source: Additionally, some dedifferentiation of muscle, bone and cartilage tissue was still observed when wound epidermis formation was prevented, although not to the same extent as normal regenerating limbs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited classical studies.

claim: Preventing wound epidermis formation led to aberrant growth factor signaling pathway activation/repression in regenerating stump tissues.
source: Preventing wound epidermis formation led to aberrant growth factor signaling pathway activation/repression in regenerating stump tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dividing cells exhibited a loss in predicted activation of canonical Wnt, HIPPO, and TGF-beta signaling when wound epidermis formation was prevented.
source: Pathway analysis revealed that while non-dividing cells exhibited no major differences, dividing cells (i.e. enriching for progenitors) exhibited a loss in predicted activation of canonical Wnt, HIPPO, and TGF-beta signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many components of canonical Wnt, HIPPO, and TGF-beta pathways were expressed at lower levels in dividing cells when wound epidermis formation was prevented.
source: Many components of these pathways were also expressed at lower levels (Figure 1C), indicating that the wound epidermis induces transcriptional activation of these pathways in dividing progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The overall transcriptional profiles of dividing progenitors in regenerating and full skin flap conditions were relatively similar.
source: Notably, the overall transcriptional profiles of dividing progenitors in both cases were relatively similar (596 differentially expressed transcripts, 313 annotated) (Supplementary file 1), signifying that while the wound epidermis activates key signaling pathways, the overall gene expression programs in early progenitors are largely wound epidermis-independent.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis data.

claim: 3911 transcripts (982 annotated) were differentially expressed in non-dividing cells in regenerating stump tissues when wound epidermis formation was prevented.
source: We found that 3911 transcripts (982 annotated) were differentially expressed in non-dividing cells in regenerating stump tissues (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary files.

claim: The majority of differentially expressed transcripts in non-dividing cells pertained to genes involved in ECM regulation, inflammation, and tissue histolysis.
source: The majority of these transcripts pertained to genes involved in ECM regulation, inflammation, and tissue histolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: Many ECM-components and regulators that maintained expression in intact and normal regenerating tissues were aberrantly down-regulated when wound epidermis formation was prevented.
source: Many ECM-components and regulators that maintained expression in intact and normal regenerating tissues were aberrantly down-regulated (e.g. fbn2, finc, has2), and regenerative ECM components as well as degrading enzymes (e.g. tenascin, mmp2, and mmp13) failed to be induced, indicating defects in ECM remodeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Components of pro-inflammatory signaling pathways including toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and interferon α/β/γ signaling were dysregulated when wound epidermis formation was prevented.
source: In particular, components of pro-inflammatory signaling pathways including toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and interferon α/β/γ signaling, as well as anti-inflammatory pathways including PPARα/RXRα signaling and anxa1 signaling were dysregulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Expression of the major bone matrix degrading enzyme catk failed to be induced when wound epidermis formation was prevented.
source: Notably, expression of the major bone matrix degrading enzyme catk failed to be induced, while the major bone and cartilage matrix component col1a1 maintained expression, indicating potential defects in bone resorption, a process that begins during the first week of regeneration (Fischman and Hay, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 1060 transcripts (480 annotated) were differentially expressed in epithelial cells when comparing wound epidermis to full skin flap conditions.
source: We found that 1060 transcripts (480 annotated) were differentially expressed (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Many transcripts involved in ECM regulation and inflammatory signaling were dysregulated in full skin flap epithelial cells.
source: Similar to the non-dividing cells in regenerating stump tissues, many transcripts involved in ECM regulation and inflammatory signaling (both pro- and anti-inflammatory) were also dysregulated in full skin flap epithelial cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Components of interferon and cytokine signaling failed to be induced in full skin flap derived epithelial cells.
source: Components of interferon and cytokine signaling failed to be induced in full skin flap derived epithelial cells, while anti-pathogenic mucins including muc5a and muc5b were overexpressed, suggesting dysregulation of inflammatory processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: mpeg1 commonly failed to be induced in the full skin flap epithelium as well as non-dividing cells in regenerating stump tissues.
source: Interestingly, mpeg1 commonly failed to be induced in the full skin flap epithelium as well as non-dividing cells in regenerating stump tissues, potentially indicating a defect in macrophage infiltration during early regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Midkine (mk) is a pleiotropic growth factor cytokine that has been shown to regulate a variety of processes including development, tumorigenesis, inflammation, and tissue repair.
source: Midkine (mk) is a pleiotropic growth factor cytokine that has been shown to regulate a variety of processes including development, tumorigenesis, inflammation, and tissue repair (Muramatsu, 2010; Weckbach et al., 2011; Gramage et al., 2015; Karaman and Alitalo, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: mk expression was induced in the wound epidermis and highly upregulated in early regenerating stump tissues.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that mk expression was induced in the wound epidermis and highly upregulated in early regenerating stump tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mk expression decreased across all transcriptionally profiled subpopulations in full skin flap sutured limbs.
source: In full skin flap sutured limbs, mk expression decreased across all transcriptionally profiled subpopulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mk failed to be transcriptionally induced in full skin flap epithelial cells.
source: Specifically, while mk expression in regenerating stump tissues was lower, mk failed to be transcriptionally induced in full skin flap epithelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data from the full skin flap experiment.

claim: mk is highly expressed during limb regeneration, but not in full skin flap sutured regenerating limbs.
source: Time course in situ hybridization of mk confirmed that it is highly expressed during limb regeneration, but not in full skin flap sutured regenerating limbs (Figure 2A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A–G.

claim: In non-regenerating intact limbs, mk was lowly expressed in cells interspersed throughout the muscle and dermis.
source: In non-regenerating intact limbs, mk was lowly expressed in cells interspersed throughout the muscle and dermis (Figure 2A–A').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A–A'.

claim: During regeneration, mk became strongly expressed in both the basal layers of the wound epidermis and mesenchymal cells within regenerating stump tissues beginning at 3 dpa.
source: During regeneration, mk became strongly expressed in both the basal layers of the wound epidermis and mesenchymal cells within regenerating stump tissues beginning at 3 dpa (Figure 2B–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B–C'.

claim: mk is first expressed in regenerating stump tissues prior to the induction of expression in the wound epidermis.
source: In situ hybridization of mk at 24 and 56 hours post-amputation (hpa) revealed a small population of mk+ cells interspersed throughout regenerating stump tissues with little to no expression of mk in the basal layers of the wound epidermis until 72 hpa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). Together, these data indicate that mk is first expressed in regenerating stump tissues prior to the induction of expression in the wound epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: During later stages of regeneration, mk expression persisted at high levels in the basal layers of the AEC and lower levels in the blastema.
source: During later stages of regeneration, mk expression persisted at high levels in the basal layers of the AEC and lower levels in the blastema (Figure 2D–F').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D–F'.

claim: MK protein is present throughout the AEC and blastema.
source: Immunostaining of axolotl MK protein further revealed the presence of MK protein throughout the AEC and blastema, providing evidence that it is indeed secreted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F'.

claim: Approximately 96.4% of mk+ expressing cells in non-regenerating tissues were comprised of prrx-1+ connective tissue cells (~43.8%), pax7+ satellite cells (~44.9%), and pecam+ endothelial cells (~7.7%).
source: Indeed, our analysis revealed that approximately 96.4% of mk+ expressing cells in non-regenerating tissues were comprised of prrx-1+ connective tissue cells (~43.8% of mk+ cells), pax7+ satellite cells (~44.9% of mk+ cells), and pecam+ endothelial cells (~7.7% of mk+ cells) (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by double in situ hybridization quantification data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: At both 3 and 7 dpa, mk-expressing cells could be divided into connective tissue cells (~53–54%), satellite cells (~36–37%), and a small percentage of endothelial cells (4–5%).
source: At both 3 and 7 dpa, mk-expressing cells could be divided into connective tissue cells (~53–54%), satellite cells (~36–37%), and a small percentage of endothelial cells (4–5%).
evidence: This claim is supported by double in situ hybridization quantification data.

claim: Only a small percentage (~9%) of mk+ cells were csf1-r+ and only 3.7% of csf1-r+ monocytes were mk+ at 5 dpa.
source: We found that only a small percentage (~9%) of mk+ cells were csf1-r+ and only 3.7% of csf1-r+ monocytes were mk+ at 5 dpa (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D), indicating mk is not predominantly expressed in monocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by double in situ hybridization quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: Treatment with iMDK beginning at either 0 or 7 dpa completely inhibited limb regeneration.
source: Treatment with iMDK beginning at either 0 or 7 dpa completely inhibited limb regeneration (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: Alcian blue staining of limbs at 60 dpa confirmed that no skeletal structures had regenerated in iMDK-treated limbs.
source: Alcian blue staining of limbs at 60 dpa confirmed that no skeletal structures had regenerated in iMDK-treated limbs (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Alcian blue staining data shown in Figure 3C–D.

claim: Mk F0 mutants exhibited delayed blastema formation and regeneration.
source: Upon amputation, mk F0 mutants exhibited delayed blastema formation and regeneration (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: The severity of delay in regeneration segregated based on genotype, with mk mosaic null animals exhibiting the most severe delay compared to control animals.
source: Notably, measurements of blastema length at 14 dpa revealed that the severity of delay in regeneration segregated based on genotype, with mk mosaic null animals (>99% mutant alleles) exhibiting the most severe delay compared to control animals (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by blastema length quantification data shown in Figure 3G–I.

claim: iMDK-treated regenerating limbs had significantly lower percentages of total EdU+ cells during late (14 dpa), but not early stages of limb regeneration (5 dpa).
source: Interestingly, iMDK-treated regenerating limbs had significantly lower percentages of total EdU+ cells during late (14 dpa), but not early stages of limb regeneration (5 dpa) (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU quantification data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Blastemal cells accumulated at the amputation plane in iMDK-treated limbs even at 40 dpa, however blastemal outgrowth never occurred.
source: Furthermore, blastemal cells accumulated at the amputation plane in iMDK-treated limbs even at 40 dpa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), however blastemal outgrowth never occurred, altogether suggesting that mk is involved in maintenance, but not induction of cellular proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significantly thinner wound epidermis was observed in both iMDK-treated and mknull mutant limbs during later stages of regeneration compared to controls.
source: In addition, we observed a significantly thinner wound epidermis in both iMDK-treated and mknull mutant limbs during later stages of regeneration compared to controls (Figure 4C–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by wound epidermis thickness quantification data shown in Figure 4C–H.

claim: The defect in AEC development was primarily attributed to higher levels of cell death in the wound epidermis in both mknull mutant and iMDK-treated regenerating limbs.
source: Further analysis of TUNEL staining in both mknull mutant and iMDK-treated regenerating limbs revealed that the defect in AEC development was primarily attributed to higher levels of cell death in the wound epidermis in both contexts (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL staining quantification data shown in Figure 5.

claim: mk mainly regulates early wound epidermis expansion by acting as a survival factor during the early wound epidermis transition to the AEC.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that mk mainly regulates early wound epidermis expansion by acting as a survival factor during the early wound epidermis transition to the AEC.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the TUNEL and wound epidermis thickness data.

claim: iMDK-treatment did not impact wound epidermis innervation.
source: Interestingly, iMDK-treatment did not impact wound epidermis innervation (Figure 6A) and data from a published microarray dataset showed similar induction of mk expression in innervated vs. denervated regenerating limbs (Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A and citation to published data.

claim: mk operates in a nerve-independent manner.
source: These results collectively indicate that mk operates in a nerve-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the innervation data and published microarray data.

claim: Sequencing of DMSO- and iMDK-treated limbs at 11 dpa revealed transcriptional dysregulation of many wound epidermis genes, suggestive of impaired functionality.
source: However, while expression of the known wound epidermis/AEC marker WE3 was observed (Figure 6A), sequencing of DMSO- and iMDK-treated limbs at 11 dpa revealed transcriptional dysregulation of many wound epidermis genes, suggestive of impaired functionality (Figure 6B–C, Supplementary file 4) (Campbell et al., 2011; Gerber et al., 2018; Leigh et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: Many pro-inflammatory pathways were enriched in iMDK-treated limbs.
source: Notably, many pro-inflammatory pathways were enriched in inhibitor treated limbs (Figure 6D–E) and both mknull mutant and iMDK-treated regenerating limbs exhibited higher monocyte densities (Figure 6F–I), suggesting that functional perturbation of mk likely leads to prolonged inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: Both mknull mutant and iMDK-treated regenerating limbs exhibited higher monocyte densities.
source: Notably, many pro-inflammatory pathways were enriched in inhibitor treated limbs (Figure 6D–E) and both mknull mutant and iMDK-treated regenerating limbs exhibited higher monocyte densities (Figure 6F–I), suggesting that functional perturbation of mk likely leads to prolonged inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by monocyte density quantification data shown in Figure 6F–I.

claim: Overexpression of mk in mknull mutant regenerating limbs rescued the delayed blastema formation and regeneration phenotype as well as the wound epidermis defects and high monocyte density.
source: Most importantly, overexpression of mk in mknull mutant regenerating limbs rescued the delayed blastema formation and regeneration phenotype as well as the wound epidermis defects and high monocyte density (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3), confirming that mk is indeed a regulator of both AEC development and the resolution of inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: iMDK-treated limbs displayed both consistently lower levels of wound epidermis proliferation as well as defects in the maintenance, but not induction, of blastemal cell proliferation in stump tissues.
source: Interestingly, iMDK-treated limbs displayed both consistently lower levels of wound epidermis proliferation as well as defects in the maintenance, but not induction, of blastemal cell proliferation in stump tissues (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: mk mutants did not exhibit any differences in the proliferation of the wound epidermis or blastemal cells, suggesting mk is not required for proliferation.
source: However, we unexpectedly did not observe any differences in the proliferation of the wound epidermis or blastemal cells of mk mutants, suggesting mk is not required for proliferation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: Overexpression of mk in regenerating limbs beginning at 3 dpa induced visible dramatic overgrowth of the wound epidermis by as early as 7 dpa.
source: Nevertheless, overexpression of mk in regenerating limbs beginning at 3 dpa induced visible dramatic overgrowth of the wound epidermis by as early as 7 dpa (Figure 7A–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–G.

claim: The expansion of the wound epidermis in mk-overexpressing limbs was attributed to a significant increase in the percentage of EdU+ cells within the wound epidermis.
source: Further analysis confirmed that this expansion was attributed to a significant increase in the percentage of EdU+ cells within the wound epidermis (Figure 7H–I), strongly suggesting that mk is sufficient, but not required, to induce proliferation in the wound epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU quantification data shown in Figure 7H–I.

claim: mk is sufficient, but not required, to induce proliferation in the wound epidermis.
source: Further analysis confirmed that this expansion was attributed to a significant increase in the percentage of EdU+ cells within the wound epidermis (Figure 7H–I), strongly suggesting that mk is sufficient, but not required, to induce proliferation in the wound epidermis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EdU data in both loss- and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Lower levels of proliferation were observed in blastemal cells of mk-overexpressing limbs.
source: We also observed lower levels of proliferation in blastemal cells of mk-overexpressing limbs (Figure 7J), indicating that high levels of mk during regeneration can have a suppressive effect on blastemal cell division.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU quantification data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: mk-overexpressing limbs displayed a persistently high monocyte density.
source: Furthermore, while control tdTomato-expressing limbs exhibited a significant decrease in monocyte density throughout regeneration, mk-overexpressing limbs displayed a persistently high monocyte density (Figure K-M), suggestive of prolonged inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by monocyte density quantification data shown in Figure 7K-M.

claim: mk levels must be tightly regulated during regeneration for proper resolution of inflammatory responses.
source: Together with our loss-of-function data, these results collectively suggest that mk levels must be tightly regulated during regeneration for proper resolution of inflammatory responses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from both loss- and gain-of-function data showing prolonged inflammation.

claim: mk-overexpressing limbs eventually regenerated with a substantial delay, gradually resolving the overgrown wound epidermis/AEC and forming a blastema.
source: Surprisingly, mk-overexpressing limbs eventually regenerated with a substantial delay, gradually resolving the overgrown wound epidermis/AEC and forming a blastema (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by time course imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of mk in intact limbs was not sufficient to affect cell proliferation or monocyte density.
source: Finally, in contrast to regeneration, overexpression of mk in intact limbs was not sufficient to affect cell proliferation or monocyte density (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the ability for mk to regulate these processes may be restricted to regenerative contexts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Transcriptional isoforms of several known mk receptors were expressed in both intact and/or early regenerating tissues.
source: We found that transcriptional isoforms of several known receptors were expressed in both intact and/or early regenerating tissues (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Several mk receptors were identified as markers for various different cell types throughout homeostasis and regeneration.
source: We also examined data from published single cell limb regeneration studies and found that several of these receptors were identified as markers for various different cell types throughout homeostasis and regeneration (Gerber et al., 2018; Leigh et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published single cell data.

claim: Syndecans (sdc-1,–2, −3,–4) and integrins (integrin alpha a4, a6, and b1) were detected at high levels in blastemal cells, basal and outer layers of the wound epidermis/AEC, endothelial cells, and schwann cells.
source: For example, syndecans (sdc-1,–2, −3,–4) and integrins (integrin alpha a4, a6, and b1) were detected at high levels in blastemal cells, basal and outer layers of the wound epidermis/AEC, endothelial cells, and schwann cells, indicating that mk likely directly signals to these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single cell data.

claim: Most mk receptors were detected at low levels or not detected at all in myeloid cells, with the exception of integrin b1, which was moderately expressed.
source: Surprisingly, most mk receptors were detected at low levels or not detected at all in myeloid cells, with the exception of integrin b1, which was moderately expressed (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single cell data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: sdc-1 was expressed in both the blastemal cells and wound epidermis during early and later stages of regeneration.
source: Interestingly, one mk receptor, sdc-1 (Mitsiadis et al., 1995b), was expressed in both the blastemal cells and wound epidermis during early and later stages of regeneration, a pattern that seemed to overlap with that of mk.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citation to published literature.

claim: Double in situ hybridization of mk with sdc-1 validated the co-expression of sdc-1 in mk+ blastemal and basal wound epidermal/AEC cells at 7 and 14 dpa.
source: Double in situ hybridization of mk with sdc-1 indeed validated the co-expression of sdc-1 in mk+ blastemal and basal wound epidermal/AEC cells at 7 and 14 dpa (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by double in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: sdc-1+ single positive cells were found in the outer layers of the wound epidermis/AEC.
source: Furthermore, sdc-1+ single positive cells were found in the outer layers of the wound epidermis/AEC, suggesting mk is capable of autocrine and paracrine signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by double in situ hybridization data.

claim: ptprz exhibited restricted expression in the wound epidermis/AEC.
source: While sdc-1 exhibited a multi-cellular expression pattern throughout regenerating tissue, we noticed that the mk receptor ptprz exhibited restricted expression in the wound epidermis/AEC (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and single cell data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Double in situ hybridization of mk and ptprz revealed low levels of ptprz expression largely restricted to the outer layers of the wound epidermis at 7 dpa.
source: Double in situ hybridization of mk and ptprz revealed low levels of ptprz expression largely restricted to the outer layers of the wound epidermis at 7 dpa.
evidence: This claim is supported by double in situ hybridization data.

claim: By 21 dpa, ptprz expression increased in the AEC and overlapped with mk expression in the basal layers.
source: By 21 dpa, ptprz expression increased in the AEC and overlapped with mk expression in the basal layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by double in situ hybridization data.

claim: ptprz failed to be up-regulated in iMDK-treated limbs, suggesting ptprz expression may rely on a mk-dependent feedback mechanism.
source: Furthermore, we noticed that ptprz failed to be up-regulated in iMDK-treated limbs, suggesting ptprz expression may rely on a mk-dependent feedback mechanism (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The global transcriptional profiles of dividing progenitors are largely wound epidermis-independent during the initial stages of regeneration.
source: The global transcriptional profiles of dividing progenitors are largely wound epidermis-independent during the initial stages of regeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNA-seq data showing relatively few differentially expressed genes in dividing cells.

claim: The transcriptional profiles of the surrounding tissues are more heavily affected when wound epidermis formation is prevented.
source: Rather, we find that the transcriptional profiles of the surrounding tissues are more heavily affected when wound epidermis formation is prevented.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNA-seq data showing many more differentially expressed genes in non-dividing cells.

claim: The early wound epidermis orchestrates the proper pro-regenerative niche during wound healing that is necessary for blastema formation by regulating early inflammation, ECM remodeling, and tissue histolysis.
source: In light of our data, we propose that the early wound epidermis orchestrates the proper pro-regenerative niche during wound healing that is necessary for blastema formation by regulating early inflammation, ECM remodeling, and tissue histolysis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the RNA-seq data showing dysregulation of these processes when wound epidermis formation is prevented.

claim: The onset of progenitor activation is stimulated by processes inherent to the injury itself such as blood clotting.
source: Given that the initial cell cycle re-entry of progenitors during regeneration is independent of the wound epidermis (Mescher, 1976; Tassava and Garling, 1979; Johnson et al., 2018), our data provide transcriptional evidence to support the notion that the onset of progenitor activation is stimulated by processes inherent to the injury itself such as blood clotting (Tanaka and Brockes, 1998; Tanaka et al., 1999; Wagner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNA-seq data and citations to published literature.

claim: The wound epidermis/AEC maintains blastemal cell proliferation by inducing and/or sustaining activation of HIPPO, canonical Wnt, and TGF-beta signaling in dividing progenitors.
source: As the wound epidermis/AEC is known to maintain blastemal cell proliferation (Mescher, 1976; Tassava and Garling, 1979), it is therefore possible that it does so by inducing and/or sustaining activation of HIPPO, canonical Wnt, and TGF-beta signaling in dividing progenitors.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the pathway analysis data and citations to published literature.

claim: The wound epidermis may play a role in macrophage recruitment during early stages of regeneration.
source: Common down-regulation of the macrophage marker mpeg1 in both the non-dividing cells and epithelia of full skin flap sutured limbs further indicates that the wound epidermis may play a role in macrophage recruitment during early stages of regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the gene expression data.

claim: The wound epidermis may mediate ECM remodeling indirectly through immune cells including macrophages.
source: Our data therefore suggest the possibility that the wound epidermis may mediate ECM remodeling indirectly through immune cells including macrophages.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the gene expression data and knowledge about macrophage function.

claim: Contact between epithelial cells and underlying regenerating stump tissues is important for proper regulation of inflammation and ECM remodeling during salamander limb regeneration.
source: Our data also indicate that contact between epithelial cells and underlying regenerating stump tissues is important for proper regulation of inflammation and ECM remodeling during salamander limb regeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the gene expression data comparing wound epidermis to full skin flap epithelia.

claim: The wound epidermis may play a role in mediating early skeletal remodeling.
source: In addition, we found signatures reminiscent of defects in bone resorption, indicating that the wound epidermis may play a role in mediating early skeletal remodeling.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the gene expression data.

claim: mk controls early wound epidermis expansion during AEC development by acting as a cell survival signal.
source: We demonstrate that mk controls early wound epidermis expansion during AEC development by acting as a cell survival signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL and wound epidermis thickness data.

claim: mk signaling through ptprz regulates cell survival.
source: In fact, mk signaling through one of its most well-studied receptors ptprz regulates cell survival (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: mk-dependent ptprz signaling similarly modulates cell survival during AEC development in limb regeneration.
source: Based on our data, it is likely that mk-dependent ptprz signaling similarly modulates cell survival during AEC development in limb regeneration given its wound epidermis-specific expression pattern.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the expression data and knowledge about ptprz function.

claim: mk induced anti-apoptotic signaling has been linked to activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade in B-cells, neurons, and cancer.
source: Furthermore, mk induced anti-apoptotic signaling has been linked to activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade in B-cells (Cohen et al., 2012), neurons (Owada et al., 1999), and cancer (Dai et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It is possible that PI3K/AKT signaling acts downstream of mk in AEC development.
source: As the inhibitor iMDK also inhibits PI3K phosphorylation (Masui et al., 2016), it is possible that PI3K/AKT signaling acts downstream of mk in AEC development.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from knowledge about iMDK and mk signaling.

claim: mk may act in concert with and/or up-stream of Wnt signaling to regulate wound epidermis development.
source: Since Wnt signaling is essential for limb regeneration and Wnt ligands are also expressed in the wound epidermis (Kawakami et al., 2006; Yokoyama et al., 2007; Ghosh et al., 2008; Knapp et al., 2013), mk may also act in concert with and/or up-stream of Wnt signaling to regulate wound epidermis development.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from knowledge about ptprz function and Wnt signaling.

claim: mk has been shown to induce proliferation of Müller glia in an autocrine manner during zebrafish photoreceptor regeneration.
source: For example, mk has been shown to induce proliferation of Müller glia in an autocrine manner during zebrafish photoreceptor regeneration (Gramage et al., 2015; Nagashima et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genetic compensation may be occurring in the mk mutant.
source: In all, these data suggested that genetic compensation may be occurring in the mutant and mk is likely not required for general proliferation or blastemal cell survival.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the differences between iMDK-treated and mutant phenotypes.

claim: mk may act in parallel with nerve-derived factors to finely control cell death/proliferation dynamics during early wound epidermis expansion.
source: Interestingly, innervation of the wound epidermis has also been shown to regulate keratinocyte proliferation in the AEC (Satoh et al., 2012). While our data suggest mk does not affect innervation, mk may act in parallel with nerve-derived factors to finely control cell death/proliferation dynamics during early wound epidermis expansion.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the data and knowledge about nerve-dependent AEC regulation.

claim: mk may act cooperatively with other secreted molecules that modulate blastema formation and growth to exert stage- and cell-type specific effects during regeneration.
source: Hence, mk may act cooperatively with other secreted molecules that modulate blastema formation and growth (Kumar et al., 2007; Currie et al., 2016; Farkas et al., 2016; Sugiura et al., 2016; Tanaka, 2016; Bryant et al., 2017b) to exert stage- and cell-type specific effects during regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the data and knowledge about other growth factors in regeneration.

claim: mk acts as an anti-inflammatory cytokine to resolve injury-induced inflammation during the initiation of limb regeneration.
source: In contrast, our data suggest that mk acts as an anti-inflammatory cytokine to resolve injury-induced inflammation during the initiation of limb regeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the monocyte density data in loss- and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Both blastemal progenitors and the wound epidermis may be additional sources of anti-inflammatory molecules including mk that aid in resolving inflammation during early stages of limb regeneration.
source: Our data further suggest that both blastemal progenitors and the wound epidermis may be additional sources of anti-inflammatory molecules including mk that aid in resolving inflammation during early stages of limb regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the expression data and functional data.

claim: mk expression may be induced by macrophage-derived factors.
source: Moreover, it is possible that mk expression may be induced by macrophage-derived factors, an interesting future avenue of investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim.

claim: mk is likely acting through both autocrine and paracrine signaling in limb regeneration.
source: Finally, both overlapping and non-overlapping expression of mk and its receptors indicates that mk is likely acting through both autocrine and paracrine signaling in limb regeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the expression data of mk and its receptors.

claim: The up-regulation of mk in blastemal progenitors and the wound epidermis may signify the re-induction of a developmental program during the initiation of limb regeneration.
source: As such, the up-regulation of mk in blastemal progenitors and the wound epidermis may signify the re-induction of a developmental program during the initiation of limb regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from knowledge about mk expression in development.

claim: mk up-regulation during the initiation of limb regeneration may depend on positive feedback signaling between mk+ blastemal progenitors and the wound epidermis.
source: Additionally, mk is first expressed in blastemal progenitors prior to the wound epidermis and failed to be strongly up-regulated when wound epidermis formation was prevented. Therefore, mk up-regulation during the initiation of limb regeneration may depend on positive feedback signaling between mk+ blastemal progenitors and the wound epidermis.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the temporal and spatial expression data.

claim: It is possible that mk secreted from blastemal progenitors may first induce mk expression in the wound epidermis through paracrine signaling, which is then self-sustained through autocrine signaling.
source: Hence, it is possible that mk secreted from blastemal progenitors may first induce mk expression in the wound epidermis through paracrine signaling, which is then self-sustained through autocrine signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the expression data and rescue experiment data.

claim: mk likely directly signals to the wound epidermis to regulate AEC development.
source: While our mk receptor expression data suggest that mk likely directly signals to the wound epidermis to regulate AEC development, how mk regulates inflammation remains less clear.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the receptor expression data.

claim: mk may regulate monocyte activity directly through low expression of receptors or as of yet unidentified receptor(s), indirectly through other tissues, or both.
source: Thus, it is possible that mk may regulate monocyte activity directly through the low expression of these or as of yet unidentified receptor(s), indirectly through other tissues, or both.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the receptor expression data in myeloid cells.

claim: mk may indirectly regulate the resolution of inflammation by stimulating the secretion of anti-inflammatory factors in tissues that then signal directly to monocytes.
source: As mk receptors are more highly expressed throughout many other cell types and tissues, it is possible that mk indirectly regulates the resolution of inflammation by stimulating the secretion of anti-inflammatory factors in these tissues that then signal directly to monocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the receptor expression data.

claim: The prolonged inflammation observed in both mk loss- and gain-of-function contexts may be indirectly or partially caused by an impaired wound epidermis/AEC.
source: As we have shown that the early wound epidermis is immunomodulatory, it is conceivable that the prolonged inflammation we observed in both mk loss- and gain-of-function contexts was indirectly or partially caused by an impaired wound epidermis/AEC, opening up the possibility that mk may regulate the resolution of inflammation in an indirect manner.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the functional data.
